name: Anthralin (dithranol)
lead: Anthralin, also called dithranol, is a synthetic topical compound from the hydroxyanthrone family, supplied as creams, ointments or pastes in strengths from roughly 0.1% to 2%. Its established medical use is plaque psoriasis.[1][2] In hair contexts it is discussed as a topical irritant treatment for patchy alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which hair falls out in round patches; people use it with the aim of regrowing hair in bald patches on the scalp, beard or brows.[1][3]

The idea behind irritant treatments such as anthralin is that mild, controlled skin irritation changes immune activity around hair follicles. A 1987 trial in 68 patients with severe alopecia areata reported a cosmetic response in 25 percent, and Wikipedia cites a 2013 review describing tentative evidence of benefit.[1][4] Pediatric and adult alopecia reviews list anthralin among available options alongside intralesional corticosteroids, minoxidil and topical immunotherapy.[3][5]
Documented effects include burning, irritation and temporary brown-to-purple staining of skin, and permanent staining of fabrics and bathroom fixtures.[1][4]

angle.text: For people with patchy alopecia areata, anthralin is an option aimed at regrowing hair in bare patches on the scalp or beard. Trials report cosmetic regrowth in a portion of patients after weeks of treatment.

paras: Anthralin is used on the skin for psoriasis. Wikipedia describes it as slower acting than topical steroids, usually taking several weeks, but without rebound flares after stopping; it is not used on the face or genitals.[1] American Academy of Dermatology guidelines on topical psoriasis therapy include it among agents with a generally high efficacy-to-safety ratio for limited disease.[2] A review of scalp psoriasis lists anthralin compounds among topical options, and a pregnancy review describes topical anthralin as among safer topical choices for localized psoriasis.[6][7]

In alopecia areata, a review chapter lists anthralin with minoxidil, topical immunotherapy and systemic immunosuppressants as options beyond intralesional corticosteroids, which it calls the treatment of choice.[5] The same chapter notes that the condition's burden is largely psychological, so treatment aims at appearance and quality of life.[5]
A pediatric alopecia areata systematic review of 122 reports covering 1,032 patients included anthralin among the treatments assessed.[3]

Reported effects include burning and irritation, which clinicians reduce by beginning with weaker preparations and increasing gradually. The compound can leave yellow-brown to purple temporary staining on skin and permanently stain clothing, shower curtains and ceramic sinks. Surrounding skin is sometimes protected with soft paraffin.[1]
In the 1987 trial every patient experienced itching and local redness with scaling.[4]

The mechanism in psoriasis is not fully understood. It is reported to accumulate in mitochondria and may generate free radicals that disrupt cellular energy and DNA replication, slowing excess cell division; anti-inflammatory effects have also been reported.[1] A 1997 review in Clinics in Dermatology covers the drug's use and properties.[8]

Anthralin appears occasionally in hair-loss discussions on T Nation, where users have posted references comparing azelaic acid and anthralin for patchy alopecia areata when discussing options for hair loss.[9][10]

A 1987 study in Archives of Dermatology treated 68 patients with severe alopecia areata using 0.5% to 1.0% anthralin cream. All experienced itching and redness; 17 patients (25%) had a cosmetic response, 12 of whom maintained it during therapy, with mean time to response of about 11 weeks for 0.5% anthralin.[4]

Wikipedia summarises a 2013 review as showing tentative evidence of benefit in alopecia areata.[1] Systematic and narrative reviews of alopecia areata treatment include anthralin among options.[3][5] Trials of anthralin for psoriasis date to at least 1979.[11]

card.summary: A skin-irritant ointment from psoriasis care that is sometimes discussed for patchy alopecia areata; evidence for hair regrowth is tentative.
card.note: Stains skin and fabrics and can burn; used under clinician direction.

quick.overview:
Anthralin (dithranol) is a topical medication mainly used for psoriasis. In hair contexts it is discussed as an irritant treatment for alopecia areata.

Wikipedia reports only tentative evidence of benefit for alopecia areata, based on a 2013 review.
quick.mechanism: It is reported to accumulate in mitochondria and generate free radicals, slowing cell division; exact action is not fully understood.
quick.risks: Burning, irritation, temporary skin staining and permanent staining of clothes and fixtures are reported. In the UK it is a Pharmacy medicine.
